name: Conjunction Fallacy
description: People can judge a detailed combined story as more probable than one of its simpler component events, because the richer story feels more representative. The classic example is rating 'Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement' as more likely than 'Linda is a bank teller.'
design_relevance_note: Relevant to personas, forecasting dashboards, risk communication, and research synthesis: teams can find a vivid, detail-rich scenario more plausible than a simpler base-rate-consistent one, which can distort prioritization and product bets.
myth_risk_note: The empirical effect is robust and multiply replicated; the caveat is a well-documented normative debate (Gigerenzer school) over whether the 'fallacy' framing is fair given ordinary-language ambiguity in how 'probability' is interpreted -- doesn't undermine the phenomenon's replicability, only its interpretation as irrationality.
prevalence_note: A classic example in behavioral economics, decision theory, and critical-thinking education; many designers know it through Kahneman/Tversky-adjacent reading even if it is not used as everyday studio jargon.

findings.description: Across multiple judgment contexts, both laypeople and experts sometimes judged a conjunction of events as more probable than one of its constituents, especially when the richer story felt more representative or easier to imagine than the logically broader alternative.
findings.source_title: Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: The conjunction fallacy in probability judgment.

applications.title: Practicing attorneys misjudge case-outcome probabilities in the Jones v. Clinton case
applications.description: Researchers Craig Fox and Richard Birke surveyed over 200 practicing attorneys (median 17 years' experience) about the real, then-ongoing Jones v. Clinton case, asking them to rate the probability of two outcomes: the case being resolved by any means other than a judicial verdict (a broader, strictly more probable category) versus the case specifically being resolved through settlement (a narrower subset of the first). Despite settlement being a logically less probable subset, the attorneys rated it as more probable -- a real-world instance of the conjunction fallacy among legal experts, not novices.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, peer-reviewed finding that even highly experienced professionals (attorneys with a median of 17 years' practice) are subject to the conjunction fallacy on a real, named case -- not a persuasion or product-design scenario. Included because it demonstrates the fallacy is not just a lab curiosity affecting novices, directly relevant to this corpus's broader myth-busting purpose around who expertise actually protects from a given bias.
